abstract: The Viral Infection Risk Indoor Simulator (VIRIS) [Xue et al. 2024] combines architectural layout, people movement, and airborne transmission modelling to predict infection risk in indoor spaces. The modelling assumptions in VIRIS include: (i) uniform aerosol concentration over the building height, allowing airborne transmission to be modelled in a two-dimensional (2D) domain, and (ii) first-order global removal of aerosols to account for surface deposition. Both assumptions lead to underestimating the infectious aerosol concentration in the breathing zone. Here, we extend VIRIS to model airborne transmission more realistically and compare the impact on infection risk predictions. We develop VIRIS-3D-L by extending the airborne transmission model in VIRIS (a reaction-diffusion equation) to three dimensions (3D) and replacing global removal with a Robin boundary condition representing localised removal due to surface deposition. We compare VIRIS and VIRIS-3D-L across three single-storey buildings with increasing architectural and people-movement complexity: a courtroom, a care home, and a supermarket. We find that VIRIS underestimates the disease transmission rate and infection risks for individuals by up to 50% relative to VIRIS-3D-L in all three buildings. However, VIRIS-3D-L requires, on average, four times the computation time of VIRIS, mainly because it extends the computational domain from a 2D surface to a 3D volume. Overall, VIRIS-3D-L provides a more realistic modelling of airborne transmission than VIRIS and is particularly suited to settings with variations in people and furniture heights and frequent 3D movement. For simpler single-storey buildings, VIRIS is suitable because of its lower computational cost.
